newsitem.title: MEXICO: Six percent growth for Mexico no pipedream, minister says.
newsitem.headline: Six percent growth for Mexico no pipedream, minister says.

text.p: Mexico's Finance Minister Guillermo Ortiz said on Sunday that he was confident of reaching the government's target of 4 percent economic growth in 1997 and that sustained growth of 6 percent a year in following years is not a pipe dream.

"Growth will be closer to 4 percent than to 3 percent in 1996," Ortiz told a breakfast meeting with international journalists, one day after the government signed a new economic pact for 1997 with labour and business leaders.
"Achieving the growth target for next year is the least controversial thing," he added. "I am not saying that growth will be 6 percent in 1998, but we can get close."
Thereafter, "growing at 6 percent a year is not wishful thinking, we have no excuse for not doing so," he said, recalling that Mexico had shown such growth rates for decades earlier this century.
Ortiz described the export-led growth target as a challenge but "we think we can do it," he said, adding that next year would be a "year of transition".
Economic recovery following the December 1994 peso crash and ensuing recession would not need a great revival in domestic consumption, Ortiz said.
He said consumption fell 14 percent in 1995 and was expected to grow about 2 percent or 3 percent this year; in 1997 it was expected to grow about 3.5 or 4 percent, he said.
"We do not need a very strong recovery (in consumption) to achieve the growth targets," he said.

Trade Minister Herminio Blanco said direct foreign investment was expected to be the same or better in 1997 compared with 1996, when foreign firms pledged to pour more than $6 billion into the Mexican economy.

Ortiz said he believed investment by Mexican firms would be considerably higher than the $6.2 billion they pledged for 1996. He said he was similary confident of hitting the 15 percent inflation target set out in the pact for next year.
He said inflation this month was expected to come in at about 1.1 to 1.2 percent.
"That is already 15 percent inflation, we are already at 15 percent inflation," he said.

An inflation bubble was expected following December price rises for gasoline and diesel fuel, he said, although smaller than last year's. December 1996 inflation was expected to be about 2 percent, he said.

Ortiz said Mexico would show a broadly balanced budget this year and that the deficit of 0.5 percent of GDP set for 1997 was not a loosening of discipline but, in fact, would require extra effort to control government spending.

That is because in 1997 the government will begin to absorb the costs of social security reform and its extensive support programmes for Mexican banks, private and business debtors, homeowners and farmers.
Further details of how the government will deal with those costs would be announced in about a week, he said.
